title: Side-Channel Attacks on Classical and Post-Quantum Cryptography: A Comparative Review
content: Cryptographic algorithms that are secure on paper can still be broken through the physical behaviour of their implementations. This problem is well studied for AES, RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography, but the migration to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) changes which operations leak and how they must be protected. This article is a structured narrative review of side-channel attacks on classical and post-quantum implementations, with attention to the standardized schemes ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA and to code-based schemes. Literature was collected from bibliographic databases and the IACR venues and extended by citation tracking; 35 experimental or analytical studies form the evidence corpus, and each is described by primitive, targeted operation, platform, leakage channel, attacker model, protection level and outcome. Instead of subjective risk ratings, every finding is graded by strength of evidence. The review shows that PQC does not invalidate established attack methods but moves leakage to new places: the number-theoretic transform, the Fujisaki–Okamoto re-encryption and comparison, signature rejection loops, compiler-generated divisions and masked domain conversions. Key or message recovery has been demonstrated against masked lattice implementations, and published first-order masked ML-KEM decapsulation is 3.5 to 3.8 times slower than the unprotected baseline on ARM Cortex-M4. The original contribution is a five-stage, literature-derived evaluation framework with a reporting template that makes results on classical and post-quantum implementations comparable.
